title: Bengaluru's Airbound Raises $37M to Build Autonomous Drones That Could Rival Trucking Costs
excerpt: The Series A round, led by Greenoaks with backing from DoorDash and Lightspeed, will fund development of larger cargo drones and expansion of a three-city delivery network in Andhra Pradesh.
body:
• Bengaluru-based Airbound has raised $37 million in Series A funding led by Greenoaks, with DoorDash, Lightspeed, and Lachy Groom participating, bringing total funding to approximately $50 million.
  • The startup has completed over 13,000 autonomous flights, including 1,000+ with Narayana Health transporting diagnostic samples between facilities in minutes instead of hours.
  • Airbound has signed an agreement with the Andhra Pradesh government for a three-city drone delivery network targeting 10,000 flights per day across retail, e-commerce, and healthcare.
  • The company aims to build drones capable of carrying up to 100 kg of cargo at costs competitive with fully loaded trucks — a goal investors say could resolve the tension between fast and cheap delivery.

Airbound, a Bengaluru-based autonomous drone startup founded in 2023, has raised $37 million in a Series A round led by Greenoaks, as it pushes to make drone delivery as cheap as trucking across India's sprawling logistics network.

The round drew participation from DoorDash, Lightspeed, Humba Ventures, and Lachy Groom — founder of robotics company Physical Intelligence — bringing Airbound's total funding to approximately $50 million. The company had previously raised $8.65 million in a seed round in October 2025, also led by Groom.

A Rocket-Like Design for Last-Mile Delivery

Airbound's drones use a vertical-flight, tail-sitter design — launching and landing like a rocket before transitioning to efficient horizontal flight. The company's current model, the TRT, weighs 3.3 pounds and carries a 2.2-pound payload. A next-generation version under development will weigh 6.6 pounds and handle up to 11 pounds. The long-term ambition is aircraft capable of hauling roughly 100 kilograms of cargo.

The startup manufactures airframes and core systems in-house at a 43,000-square-foot facility in Bengaluru and employs roughly 150 people — all while remaining pre-revenue.

"When one autonomous aircraft can move a single package with the cost efficiency of a fully loaded 20-ton truck, fast delivery and cheap delivery are no longer in tension."

— Neil Shah, Greenoaks

Proving the Model With Healthcare

Airbound has logged more than 13,000 autonomous flights across Bengaluru and Guntur, according to TechCrunch. Its most prominent operational partnership is with Narayana Health, where it has completed over 1,000 flights transporting diagnostic samples between healthcare facilities — covering 2.5 miles in approximately seven minutes, compared to three to five hours by road.

The partnership has gone far enough that Narayana's new Banashankari hospital has been designed without an on-site laboratory, planning instead to rely on Airbound's drone network for sample transport, Livemint reported.

Scaling Beyond Healthcare

The company has also signed an agreement with the Andhra Pradesh government to build a three-city drone delivery network, targeting 10,000 flights per day using 250 to 1,000 aircraft. The arrangement covers retail, e-commerce, and healthcare deliveries, though Airbound emphasizes it involves no government contracts or subsidies — only a collaborative regulatory framework.

CEO Naman Pushp has described Airbound's role as infrastructure, not operations. "That's the Boeing role — the aircraft airlines everywhere rely on, not the airline itself," he told TechCrunch.

"If you can build something that works in India, it tends to work anywhere."

— Naman Pushp, CEO, Airbound

India's Deeptech Surge

Airbound's raise comes amid a broader surge in Indian deeptech investment. Indian deeptech startups have raised $2.2 billion across 187 deals in 2026 so far, compared to $1.6 billion across 487 deals in all of 2025, according to data from Tracxn cited by Entrepreneur India. The consolidation toward larger rounds signals growing investor confidence in India's hardware and frontier technology capabilities.

The drone delivery space in India includes competitors such as Skye Air Mobility, TSAW Drones, and Garuda Aerospace, though Airbound's focus on cost parity with trucking and its vertical-flight architecture differentiate its approach. The main bottleneck across the sector remains regulation — specifically, beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) flight approvals, which limit the scale and range of autonomous drone operations.

What's Next

Airbound plans to use the Series A funding to advance its larger-payload aircraft, expand its Andhra Pradesh network, and push for the regulatory clearances needed to scale commercial operations. Pushp has signaled patience over urgency: "The goal is to be a giant in a few decades, not to make revenue as soon as we can," he told Hindu BusinessLine.

For diaspora investors and technologists tracking India's startup ecosystem, Airbound represents a bet on Indian-origin deeptech solving a global logistics challenge — autonomous, low-cost aerial delivery — with the potential to export the model well beyond India's borders.
